scope: Botanical review for exactly FL-01 through FL-10 in the US regional plant roadmap; proposed production values for main-agent review, not an automatic catalog import.

conventions.units: heightIn, spread, space and dimension evidence are real inches, never renderer pixels.
conventions.heightIn: Representative cultivated overall height including flowers, seedheads, fronds or the woody crown. It is not a foliage-only height or the largest documented wild specimen.
conventions.space: Suggested on-center garden spacing. It is a design value unless a source explicitly supplies spacing; colonizing plants can spread far beyond one modeled module.
conventions.grow: Woody-only estimated years to the stated design size, not root establishment time, lifespan or guaranteed ultimate maturity. Every value is labeled as a planning estimate in evidence.
conventions.zones: Conservative whole-zone USDA cultivation ranges synthesized from the cited Florida horticultural sources. Zone overlap alone does not establish heat, humidity, local provenance or legal suitability.
conventions.bloomMonths: Approximate Florida flowering windows. Year-round means a warm, frost-free setting; cooler Florida sites can have shorter windows. A grass seedhead is represented as bloom only when a seasonal source supports it; cycads have cones and bloomMonths is empty.
conventions.taxonomy: The latin field retains the exact species-level roadmap target. Synonyms are selected discovery aliases, not exhaustive nomenclature; infraspecific and lookalike cautions remain explicit.
conventions.persistence: Biological information for authoring descriptions and seasonal colors. No Phase 0 climate, native-origin, legal-filter or seasonal-engine change is authorized by this file.
conventions.limits: Do not turn Florida occurrence into a statewide-local claim. NativeTo and provenance use the current broad contract only; county/ecotype suitability remains text. Do not infer deer, rabbit, human-edibility or pet-safety ratings from this review.

evidence.taxonomy: Kew accepts Phyla nodiflora and lists Lippia nodiflora and Verbena nodiflora as homotypic synonyms; its recognized varieties have much broader geography than a Florida-local claim.
evidence.dimensions: UF/IFAS separates foliage to 3 in from flowers to 6 in. Long stolons root at nodes and one unrestricted plant may extend 8–10 ft; proposed 36-in spread is a modeled garden patch, not a biological colony limit.
evidence.spacing: UF/IFAS directly recommends transplant divisions 12 in apart, so the space value has strong numerical support.
evidence.hardinessAndCulture: UF/IFAS gives 8A–11, full sun to partial shade, and moist through not-extremely-dry soils with drought tolerance after establishment. Full and medium are the primary authoring choices.
evidence.floweringAndPersistence: UF Gardening Solutions gives May–October; the lawn-plant review notes favorable sites can flower longer. Long-lived stoloniferous herbaceous perennial, with winter or drought dormancy possible and warm-season return.
evidence.numericalConfidence: High for height, spacing and zones; moderate for the deliberately bounded spread module.

caveats: Keep barriers or regular edging in the blurb: the static spread field cannot represent continuing stolon spread into beds.

evidence.taxonomy: Kew accepts Mimosa strigillosa. No obsolete scientific alias is needed for catalog discovery; powderpuff and herbaceous mimosa are common names.
evidence.dimensions: USDA describes a 6–8-in stoloniferous plant. FNPS reports 3–6-in mats capable of spreading roughly 100 ft; proposed 48-in spread is a design module rather than a mature colony endpoint.
evidence.spacing: FNPS cultivation guidance places potted plants 2–4 ft apart and reports rapid fill; proposed 36 in is the midpoint and has moderate support because plug size and desired closure time vary.
evidence.hardinessAndCulture: UF's native-bee guide gives 8–11. Full sun is primary; the plant accepts part sun and typically moist soils, becoming drought tolerant after establishment.
evidence.floweringAndPersistence: FNPS gives spring through fall and long-lived perennial persistence. Foliage may remain but becomes sparse from late fall into early spring; another UF account describes disappearance in the coolest months, so cold exposure controls the visible result.
evidence.numericalConfidence: High for overall height and zones; moderate for spacing; spread is a bounded colony module.

evidence.taxonomy: Kew accepts Helianthus debilis and five subspecies. Florida horticulture includes subsp. debilis on the east coast, subsp. vestitus on the west coast and subsp. cucumerifolius in other sandy settings; the roadmap remains species-level.
evidence.dimensions: UF gives a broad species value of 24–48 in tall and wide, but specifically reports about 18 in in its beach-groundcover use. Proposed 18 by 48 in represents that roadmap role; some forms can be taller and east-coast colonies much wider.
evidence.spacing: UF directly gives 18–24 in; proposed 24 in favors a looser, drought-adapted planting.
evidence.hardinessAndCulture: FNPS gives subsp. debilis 8B–11; proposed whole-zone 9–11 is a conservative rounding. Full sun, sharply drained sand and dry primary moisture are well supported; overwatering can cause decline.
evidence.floweringAndPersistence: UF calls flowering year-round and semi-evergreen in suitable Florida sites. FNPS calls east-coast material deciduous and short-lived, blooming most of the year in its natural range; freezing sites can treat it as an annual/reseeder.
evidence.numericalConfidence: High for spacing; moderate for the role-specific height and whole-zone rounding because the species aggregates distinct subspecies.

Florida database recognition of debilis, vestitus and cucumerifolius subspecies

caveats: Source locally appropriate, correctly identified stock. FNPS explicitly warns not to common-garden Helianthus debilis subspecies because of introgression.
Year-round bloom is a frost-free Florida representation, not a nationwide promise. Cooler sites can lose plants and rely on seedlings.
Do not turn species-level dimensions into a claim that every subspecies remains 18 in high.

evidence.taxonomy: Kew accepts Eragrostis elliottii; obsolete Poa nitida and Eragrostis nitida are illegitimate names and are not useful catalog aliases.
evidence.dimensions: FNPS gives 12–36 in high by 12–24 in wide. Kew's GrassBase description gives flowering culms about 16–31 in; proposed 36 in captures the airy top of a vigorous cultivated clump.
evidence.spacing: No primary source supplied garden on-center spacing. Proposed 18 in is a moderate-confidence design estimate within the mature 12–24-in crown width.
evidence.hardinessAndCulture: FNPS lists 8A–10B, full sun and usually-moist through not-extremely-dry soils. Medium is primary even though established plants tolerate dry intervals.
evidence.floweringAndPersistence: FNPS describes a short-lived perennial dense clump, winter dormant, with fall bloom. September–November is a calendar translation of fall, not month-level field data.
evidence.numericalConfidence: High for overall size and zones; moderate for spacing; weak-to-moderate for exact bloom months.

sources.supports: overall dimensions, short-lived clump, winter dormancy, fall bloom, light, moisture and zones 8A–10B

caveats: Render a low blue-green/silver foliage clump with a fine airy flowering haze; 36 in is the flower/seedhead envelope, not a solid foliage ball.
Short-lived means renewal or reseeding may be needed; do not describe it as an indefinitely permanent isolated tussock.
High salt-spray tolerance does not mean tolerance of brackish inundation.

evidence.taxonomy: Kew accepts Tripsacum floridanum and gives Tripsacum dactyloides var. floridanum as its homotypic synonym. It must remain distinct from the much larger T. dactyloides.
evidence.dimensions: FNPS and UF give 24–36 in high and wide. That overall value includes the modest terminal flower/seed structures; separate foliage-only and flowering heights were not verified.
evidence.spacing: No primary source supplied an on-center value. Proposed 36 in matches the mature clump width and is a moderate design estimate.
evidence.hardinessAndCulture: FNPS lists 8A–10B, full to part sun, lime-rock or sandy sites and somewhat moist through very dry conditions. Full and dry fit the pine-rockland roadmap role, but this species is adaptable rather than strictly xeric.
evidence.floweringAndPersistence: FNPS calls it an evergreen, clump-forming, short-lived perennial that can look messy after cold spells. UF discusses its brown flower stalks in a summer-perennial feature; June–August is a weak calendar translation rather than exact phenology data.
evidence.numericalConfidence: High for size and zones; moderate for spacing; weak for exact bloom months.

evidence.taxonomy: Kew accepts Stachytarpheta jamaicensis. Florida's 2026 flora separately recognizes S. cayennensis, S. urticifolia and named hybrids, including S. ×intercedens (jamaicensis × urticifolia); they are not aliases.
evidence.dimensions: FNPS gives the native trailing form 6–12 in high by 36–48 in wide. Florida Museum allows up to 36 in, reflecting variable material; proposed 12 in deliberately represents the low native groundcover target rather than tall retail porterweed.
evidence.spacing: UF gives 36–60-in spacing in a fact sheet whose 4–8-ft size appears inconsistent with low native material. Proposed 36 in uses only the lower direct spacing bound; confidence is moderate.
evidence.hardinessAndCulture: FNPS gives 8B–11; UF Orange County gives 9B–11 for the low native groundcover. Proposed 9–11 is conservative. Full sun and dry, freely draining soil are primary, with part sun and establishment irrigation possible.
evidence.floweringAndPersistence: FNPS and Florida Museum report all-year bloom in warm conditions. FNPS calls it evergreen and short-lived at roughly five years; a UF Pinellas guide reports winter dormancy, so foliage persistence depends on cold exposure.
evidence.numericalConfidence: High for the low-form height/spread and zones; moderate for spacing because the available direct spacing source may contain mixed horticultural material.

Do not use UF/IFAS FP559's 4–8-ft dimensions for this low native record; its text conflicts with FNPS and low-form UF guidance and likely reflects mixed horticultural material.

evidence.taxonomy: Kew accepts Zamia integrifolia with several accepted varieties. FNPS lists Z. floridana and Z. pumila as horticultural synonyms, but modern treatments split or rank this complex differently; keep them as searchable legacy aliases, not proof that all Caribbean Z. pumila is the same plant.
evidence.dimensions: FNPS gives 24–36 in high by 36–60 in wide; proposed 36 by 60 in uses the full straight-species crown. Height is evergreen fronds from a mostly subterranean caudex. This gymnosperm bears cones, not flowers.
evidence.spacing: No direct garden spacing was verified. Proposed 48 in allows mature fronds to overlap within the 60-in crown and is a moderate design estimate.
evidence.hardinessAndCulture: UF gives 8B–11 and FNPS gives 8A–11. Part sun and dry, well-drained soil are primary; established plants tolerate full sun and need little irrigation.
evidence.floweringAndPersistence: Evergreen, long-lived, dioecious cycad; bloomMonths must remain empty because the reproductive structures are male and female cones.
evidence.growConfidence: Moderate ten-year design estimate. UF describes very slow growth and reports roughly a decade to a harvestable plant, but that is not a controlled time-to-36-by-60-in trial.

caveats: All parts are poisonous and the seeds are especially toxic; do not present historical starch use as household food preparation advice.
Florida regulates native Zamia as commercially exploited. Use propagated nursery stock; do not collect wild plants or plant parts without applicable permits.
Needs a cycad morphology. Keep type shrub for its persistent hard crown/footprint; it is neither a palm nor a flowering fern.
The ten-year grow field is an explicit planning estimate with weaker numerical evidence than the mature dimensions.

evidence.taxonomy: Kew accepts Hamelia patens and lists Hamelia erecta as a synonym. Florida straight native material is commonly treated as H. patens var. patens; H. patens var. glabra and plants sold as Compacta/Dwarf require separate provenance review.
evidence.dimensions: UF gives 72–144 in high by 60–96 in wide; FNPS records an ultimate potential near 240 by 120 in. Proposed 144 by 96 in is a representative unpruned landscape shrub rather than the wild maximum or a compact cultivar.
evidence.spacing: No direct spacing was verified. Proposed 96 in matches the selected crown width and is a moderate design estimate.
evidence.hardinessAndCulture: UF and FNPS support 9–11, full to part sun and well-drained medium-to-dry soil. Full sun is primary for the strongest flowering.
evidence.floweringAndPersistence: FNPS reports semi-evergreen and all-year bloom unless frozen; zone-9 plants can die back and usually resprout. The year-round calendar is therefore a frost-free representation.
evidence.growConfidence: Moderate four-year design estimate. UF calls growth fast and documents roughly 1-ft nursery plants reaching 5 ft in one warm season; no direct time-to-12-ft study was found.

evidence.taxonomy: Kew accepts Serenoa repens and lists Serenoa serrulata among its synonyms. Naturally blue-green or silver foliage is intraspecific variation, not a reason to create an undocumented cultivar record.
evidence.dimensions: UF's palm guide gives a typical 72 by 144-in clump; its species sheet gives 36–72-in height with 36–60-in fan leaves. FNPS notes larger old plants. Proposed dimensions represent a substantial landscape clump, not the indefinite rhizomatous colony.
evidence.spacing: No direct ornamental spacing was verified. Proposed 120 in allows some fan overlap within the 144-in clump and is a weak-to-moderate design estimate.
evidence.hardinessAndCulture: UF's species sheet gives 8A–11A, moderate-to-high light, wide soil adaptability and high drought tolerance. Full and dry are primary while part sun and periodically moist habitats remain possible.
evidence.floweringAndPersistence: UF reports spring bloom, with 24–36-in inflorescences intertwined within the leaves rather than extending overall height. March–June is a broad Florida calendar translation and lacks exact month-level field evidence. Evergreen, creeping-rhizomatous, very slow and exceptionally long-lived.
evidence.growConfidence: Weak twenty-year design estimate to a 6-by-12-ft represented clump. Sources establish very slow growth and extreme longevity but do not provide time-to-size; old clonal expansion continues far beyond this horizon.

caveats: Needs a low fan-palm morphology with creeping/subterranean trunks. Keep type shrub so the persistent clump reserves its footprint; this is not an underplantable single-trunk tree.
Backward-pointing petiole teeth are a physical hazard and should appear in the blurb.
Colonies can outlive and outgrow one modeled crown. The 20-year grow and 120-in spacing fields have weak numerical support and are planning estimates.

evidence.taxonomy: Kew accepts Myrcianthes fragrans and lists Eugenia fragrans and Myrcianthes simpsonii as synonyms. Straight species values must not be replaced by the separate Compacta cultivar.
evidence.dimensions: UF gives 60–144 in high by 36–60 in wide for a landscape shrub and elsewhere reports occasional 20-ft specimens; FNPS gives 60–240 by 36–180 in. Proposed 144 by 60 in follows UF's representative straight-species screen rather than the largest tree-form crown.
evidence.spacing: No direct on-center spacing was verified. Proposed 60 in matches the selected mature shrub width and has moderate design confidence.
evidence.hardinessAndCulture: FNPS lists 10A–11, full to part sun and somewhat moist through not-extremely-dry soils, often on limestone/calcareous substrate. Part and medium are primary for the hammock-screen role.
evidence.floweringAndPersistence: FNPS reports evergreen, long-lived growth and sporadic flowers throughout the year, strongest in spring and early summer. March–June encodes the primary display rather than every incidental flower.
evidence.growConfidence: Weak-to-moderate twelve-year design estimate. UF reports slow to moderate growth, but no direct time-to-12-ft maturity study was found.
